attribute_types.label: abundance
attribute_types.description: A subjective description of the abundance of organisms, conspecific with the cataloged item, at the collecting locality.

attribute_types.label: age
attribute_types.description: The length of time or stage or state that an organism has lived or an object has existed. This is a free text field so specificity is recommended. If general age groups are desired (e.g., adult, juvenile, subadult, etc), please see life stage and its values. If specific numeric age is known, use numeric age.

attribute_types.label: antler circumference
attribute_types.description: Antler circumference at the lowest point on the antler beam, above the burr.

attribute_types.label: antler diameter
attribute_types.description: Antler diameter at the lowest point on the antler beam, above the burr.

attribute_types.label: antler points
attribute_types.description: Total number of points on one (method = left or right) or both (method = total) antlers that are at least 1” in length, including the tips of the beams. Total, left, or right should be included in method to provide details about what the count describes.

attribute_types.label: antler spread
attribute_types.description: Distance between antlers. Method should be given. For example, "measurements per: https://www.boone-crockett.org/scorechart/add/whitetail_deer."

attribute_types.label: archaeological feature
attribute_types.description: Archaeological features such as a fire pit, hearth, house foundation, etc. Something that a person made but then left behind at an archaeological site.

attribute_types.label: associated species
attribute_types.description: Free-text description of species associated with the specimen.

attribute_types.label: axillary girth
attribute_types.description: The circumference measured around the body directly subordinate to the limbs at the site of the axillaries (e.g., armpits).

attribute_types.label: behavior
attribute_types.description: The way in which an animal acts in response to a particular situation or stimulus.

attribute_types.label: bill depth
attribute_types.description: Length from the top of the upper mandible to the base of the lower mandible measured at the deepest point, either at the bill base or gonys.

attribute_types.label: bill length
attribute_types.description: A measure of a bill that should be described in Methods. See also Culmen Length for a more specific term.

attribute_types.label: bill width
attribute_types.description: Width of the bill measured at the anterior margin of the nares.

attribute_types.label: body condition
attribute_types.description: General description of body condition.

attribute_types.label: body temperature
attribute_types.description: The body temperature of an animal.

attribute_types.label: body width
attribute_types.description: Measured with calipers from left side to right side in mm or cm, at the widest point of the body (e.g., belly).

attribute_types.label: breadth
attribute_types.description: Widest part of the narrow axis of a whole egg.

attribute_types.label: brood patch
attribute_types.description: Information about the presence of and/or general description of a featherless, fluid-filled area on the abdomen or breast of birds that is filled with surface blood vessels which are used to apply heat to the eggs during incubation.

attribute_types.label: bursa
attribute_types.description: General description of the bursa.

attribute_types.label: bursa length
attribute_types.description: Length measurement of the bursa. Specify means of measurement in Methods.

attribute_types.label: bursa width
attribute_types.description: Width measurement of the bursa. Specify means of measurement in Methods.

attribute_types.label: calcar length
attribute_types.description: Length of a spur of cartilage and/or bone arising from inner side of ankle and running along part of outer interfemoral membrane in bats.

attribute_types.label: carapace length
attribute_types.description: Length of carapace, straight or curved not specified.

attribute_types.label: caste
attribute_types.description: The group of individuals within the same species of social insects that have a different appearance. This appearance is usually related to the role of that caste within the colony. Values are controlled by the Caste Code Table.

attribute_types.label: chromatography compound
attribute_types.description: Identified compound present in a given mixture, using the thin-layer chromatography technique.

attribute_types.label: clutch size
attribute_types.description: Number of eggs laid in a discrete group within a clearly defined, often elaborate, nest. (after "A Dictionary of BIRDS", edited by Bruce Campbell and Elizabeth Lack, 1985)

attribute_types.label: clutch size of nest parasite
attribute_types.description: Number of eggs belonging to avian nest parasite (e.g., cowbird).

attribute_types.label: colors
attribute_types.description: General description of colors.

attribute_types.label: copyright notice
attribute_types.description: A notation attached to a creative work indicating the copyright owner of a work. The copyright notice may take a variety of forms depending on applicable law. In the United States the most common form is © [year of first publication] [name of copyright holder].

attribute_types.label: copyright status
attribute_types.description: Describes the rights of the copyright holder listed for the object.

attribute_types.label: credit line
attribute_types.description: A brief statement indicating how the work came into the current or an earlier collection or how it came to be on view at the repository.

attribute_types.label: crop contents
attribute_types.description: Dietary contents contained in the crop of birds.

attribute_types.label: crown-rump length
attribute_types.description: Crown rump length (CRL) is the length from the top of the head to bottom of the torso.

attribute_types.label: crystal habit
attribute_types.description: In mineralogy, crystal habit is the characteristic external shape of an individual crystal or crystal group. A single crystal's habit is a description of its general shape and its crystallographic forms, and how well developed each form is.

attribute_types.label: culmen length
attribute_types.description: Chord measurement along the dorsal ridge of the upper mandible from the tip of the bill to the feathering at base of the bill. For birds of prey, culmen length is measured from the tip of the bill to the anterior edge of the cere.

attribute_types.label: culture of origin
attribute_types.description: Cultural affiliation of object creator.

attribute_types.label: culture of use
attribute_types.description: Cultural affiliation of object user.

attribute_types.label: curved carapace length
attribute_types.description: Carapace length measured across curved surface.

attribute_types.label: curvilinear length
attribute_types.description: Measurement from the crown of head to the crown of the rump in a fetus. It is also possible to use curvilinear length when a linear measurement is not possible, as with a frozen carcass, which mirrors the traditional total length measurement (nose to tail tip).

attribute_types.label: dentition
attribute_types.description: A free text field describing the development, arrangement, or condition of the teeth or tooth. Specificity, counts, and measurements are encouraged.

attribute_types.label: description
attribute_types.description: Description of the object, specimen, or observation.

attribute_types.label: detected
attribute_types.description: The attribute value was detected.

attribute_types.label: dimensions
attribute_types.description: Dimensions of the object (height x width x depth).

attribute_types.label: diploid number
attribute_types.description: A number that represents the number of pairs of homologous copies of each chromosome that are present.

attribute_types.label: duration
attribute_types.description: Total duration of an audiovisual item as expressed in minutes and seconds. For example: 148 minutes

attribute_types.label: ear from crown
attribute_types.description: Length of the ear from the crown to the tip.

attribute_types.label: ear from notch
attribute_types.description: Length of the ear from the notch to the tip.

attribute_types.label: eggshell thickness
attribute_types.description: A measurement of eggshell thickness generally representing the average thickness gauged at both poles and equator.

attribute_types.label: electrical conductivity
attribute_types.description: The ability or power to conduct or transmit heat, electricity, or sound through a substance.

attribute_types.label: examined for
attribute_types.description: A systematic examination for the attribute value was made.

attribute_types.label: exhibit caption
attribute_types.description: Text of a label describing the object when exhibited in a museum or other public space.

attribute_types.label: experimental
attribute_types.description: Is there any reason that this organism and its host do not represent a natural occurence?

attribute_types.label: fat deposition
attribute_types.description: General description of fat deposition.

attribute_types.label: forearm length
attribute_types.description: Length of the forelimb between the elbow and wrist.

attribute_types.label: fork length
attribute_types.description: Fork length (FL) is the length of a fish measured from the tip of the snout to the end of the middle caudal fin rays and is used in fishes in which it is difficult to tell where the vertebral column ends. It is also considered a more suitable measurement for fish with forked caudal fins.

attribute_types.label: format
attribute_types.description: The file format format, physical medium, or dimensions of the resource following the National Archives Format Authority List.

attribute_types.label: frame rate
attribute_types.description: Frame rate (commonly expressed in frames per second or FPS) is typically the frequency at which consecutive images are captured or displayed. This definition applies to film and video cameras, computer animation, and motion capture systems.

attribute_types.label: framed
attribute_types.description: Is the object framed? Yes or No.

attribute_types.label: gape width
attribute_types.description: Width of the bill measured across the widest point at the base.

attribute_types.label: gonad length
attribute_types.description: Measurement of the long axis of the gonad (which may be testes or ovary and can be indicated in Remarks or by implication of attribute of sex). Left or right side gonad should be indicated in the Methods.

attribute_types.label: gonad weight
attribute_types.description: Weight measurement of the gonad (which may be testes or ovary and can be indicated in Remarks or by implication of attribute of sex). Left or right side gonad should be indicated in the Methods.

attribute_types.label: gonad width
attribute_types.description: Measurement of the short axis of the gonad (testis in males; ovary in females). The side measured (left or right) should be indicated in the Methods if known.

attribute_types.label: hallux length
attribute_types.description: Length of hallux as measured from base of Digit I on hind limb to base of claw.

attribute_types.label: head length
attribute_types.description: Maximum chord length of the head along the dorsal midline, measured from the tip of the rostrum to the back of the head.

attribute_types.label: head width
attribute_types.description: A measurement of the width of the head taken at the widest part of the head.

attribute_types.label: height
attribute_types.description: Height of the specimen.

attribute_types.label: hind foot with claw
attribute_types.description: Length of the hind foot from the back of the ankle to the tip of the longest claw. A numeric value plus units.

attribute_types.label: hind foot without claw
attribute_types.description: Length of the hind foot from the back of the ankle to the base of the longest claw. A numeric value plus units.

attribute_types.label: hind limb length
attribute_types.description: Total length of the femur, tibia/fibula, tarsals, metatarsals and toes.

attribute_types.label: historical
attribute_types.description: Is an item historical (vs. ethnological)?

attribute_types.label: incubation stage
attribute_types.description: General description of the stage of development of the egg or embryo within the egg.

attribute_types.label: Indigenous term
attribute_types.description: Indigenous language term for a given object and/or material type.

attribute_types.label: individual count
attribute_types.description: The number of individual organisms represented by the catalog record.

attribute_types.label: inscriptions and marks
attribute_types.description: Inscriptions and or marks found on the object.

attribute_types.label: isotope value
attribute_types.description: The abundance of certain stable isotopes and chemical elements within organic and inorganic compounds.

attribute_types.label: keywords
attribute_types.description: Keywords relevant to the object. Mainly used for migration from legacy database, i.e., exists in an older database, may be discarded later.

attribute_types.label: language
attribute_types.description: Language of record as registered on Glottolog.

attribute_types.label: life stage
attribute_types.description: The developmental stage of the life cycle of the organism represented.

attribute_types.label: location in host
attribute_types.description: Verbatim description of the anatomical location of the parasite in or on the host.

attribute_types.label: luster
attribute_types.description: Lustre (luster; US English) or l is the way light interacts with the surface of a crystal, rock, or mineral.

attribute_types.label: materials
attribute_types.description: Materials used in the construction of the object. (These data will be normalized and standardized as cultural collection development continues.)

attribute_types.label: maximum standard length
attribute_types.description:
Length of the largest individual in a lot of fish measured from the tip of the
snout to the end of the last vertebra or posterior end of caudal peduncle. Do not use for individuals.

attribute_types.label: maximum total length
attribute_types.description:
In fish length of the largest individual in a lot measured from the tip of the
snout to tip of the longest lobe of caudal fin. Measurement done with
caudal fin lobes compressed and measured at midline. Do not use for individuals.

attribute_types.label: middle toe length
attribute_types.description: Length of the middle toe as measured from base of Digit III on hind limb to base of claw.

attribute_types.label: minimum standard length
attribute_types.description:
Length of the smallest individual in a lot of fish measured from the tip of the
snout to the end of the last vertebra or posterior end of caudal peduncle. Do not use for individuals.

attribute_types.label: minimum total length
attribute_types.description: In fish length of the smallest individual in a lot measured from the tip of the snout to tip of the longest lobe of caudal fin. Measurement done with caudal fin lobes compressed and measured at midline. Do not use for individuals.

attribute_types.label: molt condition
attribute_types.description: General description of molt stage or condition.

attribute_types.label: mortality cause
attribute_types.description: The means that resulted in or contributed to the death of the cataloged organism, and may include the circumstances of the act that produced any such fatal injuries.

attribute_types.label: neck width
attribute_types.description: Measured with calipers from left side to right side in mm or cm. The neck would probably be at the narrowest point.

attribute_types.label: nest description
attribute_types.description: A description of the nest itself (e.g., "Nest is a small cup made of grasses"), not the placement (e.g., 6 ft in willow tree) which should go into habitat.

attribute_types.label: nest phenology
attribute_types.description: Comments about timing of nest building and egg laying.

attribute_types.label: not detected
attribute_types.description: The attribute value was not detected.

attribute_types.label: not examined for
attribute_types.description: The record was not examined for the given value.

attribute_types.label: number of labels
attribute_types.description: A value that represents the number of labels associated with the object.

attribute_types.label: numeric age
attribute_types.description: Age of specimen given as a numeric value plus units.

attribute_types.label: object title
attribute_types.description: Title of the object that may be different from the title used in Identification.

attribute_types.label: ovum
attribute_types.description: A measurement of the female reproductive cell, or gamete.

attribute_types.label: parts examined
attribute_types.description: Organs, cavities, surfaces, and locations examined for the possibility of parasites.

attribute_types.label: pit depth
attribute_types.description: Depth under the ground surface; free-text field.

attribute_types.label: plastron length
attribute_types.description: Length of plastron.

attribute_types.label: portfolio or series
attribute_types.description: A portfolio is a number of prints presented as a group and often, though not necessarily, by the same artist and based on a related theme. A series can be defined as more than one related work grouped by the artist or in some logical way. Use if there is a title for the portfolio or series.

attribute_types.label: processing history
attribute_types.description: Provides information about when and how a cataloged item was processed or handled (inventoried, cataloged, verified, etc.).

attribute_types.label: provenience
attribute_types.description: The general location within an archaeological site where an object was collected.

attribute_types.label: provenience east
attribute_types.description: The exact east coordinate within an archaeological site where an object was collected.

attribute_types.label: provenience north
attribute_types.description: The exact north coordinate within an archaeological site where an object was collected.

attribute_types.label: quadrant
attribute_types.description: The quadrant within an archaeological test unit where an object was collected from. During an archaeological excavation test units are split into four equal quads and then each quad is excavated separately.

attribute_types.label: radiometric date
attribute_types.description: Age derived from radioisotope methodology.

attribute_types.label: reproductive data
attribute_types.description: General description of reproductive data.

attribute_types.label: sex
attribute_types.description: Sex of the organism.

attribute_types.label: skull ossification
attribute_types.description: Description or degree of skull pneumaticity.

attribute_types.label: snout-vent length
attribute_types.description: Length from tip of the snout to the most posterior opening of the cloacal slit (vent), commonly used in herpetology. Best practice will include means of measurement in Methods.

attribute_types.label: spleen length
attribute_types.description: Length of spleen; abnormal size may be a marker of infection or pregnancy.

attribute_types.label: square
attribute_types.description: Archaeological test unit an object was collected from.

attribute_types.label: standard length
attribute_types.description:
Standard Length (SL) is the length of a fish measured from the tip of the
snout to the end of the last vertebra or posterior end of caudal peduncle.

attribute_types.label: stomach contents
attribute_types.description: General description of the specimen's gut contents.

attribute_types.label: straight carapace length
attribute_types.description: Carapace length measured as straight line across curved surface.

attribute_types.label: stratigraphic position
attribute_types.description: natural stratigraphic layer an archaeological object was collected from

attribute_types.label: subject matter
attribute_types.description: The subject matter of a work of art (sometimes referred to as its content) is the narrative, iconographic, or non-objective meaning conveyed by an abstract or a figurative composition. It is what is depicted in and by a work of art. It also covers the function of an object or architecture that otherwise has no narrative content. Formerly subject, a topic of the resource.

attribute_types.label: tail base width
attribute_types.description: A measure of the width of the tail at the location where the tail meets the torso.

attribute_types.label: tail condition
attribute_types.description: A general description of the condition of the tail.

attribute_types.label: tail girth
attribute_types.description: A measure of the full circumference of the tail at the location described in method.

attribute_types.label: tail length
attribute_types.description: Length of tail.

attribute_types.label: tarsus length
attribute_types.description: Length measurement of the tarsus. Birds: Chord length of the tarsometatarsus, measured from the back of its articulation with the tibiotarsus to the base of the toes on the top of the foot.

attribute_types.label: thumb length with claw
attribute_types.description: The length of the first digit (pollex) of the mammalian forelimb, with claw (e.g. for bats)

attribute_types.label: tooth length
attribute_types.description: anteroposterior tooth length, a measurement of the maximum distance between the anterior and posterior surfaces of the tooth.

attribute_types.label: tooth width
attribute_types.description: a measurement of the tranverse width: the maximum distance between the medial and lateral surfaces of the tooth.

attribute_types.label: total length
attribute_types.description: Total length of the item.

attribute_types.label: tragus length
attribute_types.description: Standard measurement for bats.

attribute_types.label: unformatted measurements
attribute_types.description: Text regarding measurements of the specimen (usually biological individual). Use more specific attributes when possible.

attribute_types.label: user contributed comments
attribute_types.description: Comments associated with the specimen that are contributed by users of the collection. May or may not be part of the original documentation. Submitted to or collected by collection staff and subject to curatorial approval.

attribute_types.label: verbatim agent
attribute_types.description: Verbatim agent accepts any string value. This attribute should be used when there is little to no information about a collector or preparator instead of creating a low-information agent (no dates, relationships, or addresses are known for the agent). Indicate the agent role with regard to the catalog object in the attribute method.

attribute_types.label: verbatim attribute
attribute_types.description: The values entered in this attribute should represent structured data about a catalog record that does not fit into an existing attribute. Over time, use of structured terms may result in creation of a new attribute if the community deems it valuable. If units are required, they should be part of the free-text structure.

attribute_types.label: verbatim host age
attribute_types.description: Parasite host's age as described by collector or preparator.

attribute_types.label: verbatim host ID
attribute_types.description: The description of the host's taxonomic identity exactly as provided by the original documentation of the specimen. These will vary from explicit scientific names to vague common names.

attribute_types.label: verbatim host sex
attribute_types.description: Parasite host's sex as recorded by collector or preparator.

attribute_types.label: verbatim preservation date
attribute_types.description: The date the specimen ceased to grow and change, as opposed to the date when it was collected.  Often the date of death. Avoid this in favor of additional specimen_event determinations.

attribute_types.label: virulence gene index
attribute_types.description: Virulence gene index refers to multi-virulence gene index, MVGI (the number of virulence genes detected in one strain/total number of detected virulence genes) and is recorded as a ratio of the number of virulence genes expressed in the specimen (see Deng et al 2020). Pathogenic bacteria virulence genes are specific genetic components that enable bacteria to cause disease by enhancing their ability to invade host tissues, evade the immune system, and obtain nutrients from the host. These genes encode various factors such as toxins, adhesion molecules, and enzymes that contribute to the bacteria’s pathogenicity. (example of values: 4/5; 5/5; 3/7) Method and date is needed for each entry.

attribute_types.label: weight
attribute_types.description: Total body or object weight.

attribute_types.label: width
attribute_types.description: Width of the specimen or object.

attribute_types.label: wing chord
attribute_types.description: Measured from the bend of the wing to the tip of the longest primary feathers. Often the wings and feathers may be flattened so that the measure is maximized but in some cases the chord length with natural curvature is preferred (note in Methods).

attribute_types.label: wing span
attribute_types.description: The distance from one wingtip to the other wingtip.

attribute_types.label: year class
attribute_types.description: All of the fish of any species or population hatched during one annual spawning period, with members of the same year class generally treated as if they were hatched on the same day for analytical purposes.

ctcaste.description: Drones are male bees from colonies of social bees.
The primary reproductive female caste of social insects (especially ants, wasps, and bees of order Hymenoptera, as well as termites). Gynes are those destined to become queens.
In termites, the king helps found the colony with the queen and will continue to mate with the queen during his life.
In some species the workers and soldiers are dimorphic (of two sizes), with the larger individuals called major soldiers or workers and the smaller ones called minor soldiers or workers
In some species the workers and soldiers are dimorphic (of two sizes), with the larger individuals called major soldiers or workers and the smaller ones called minor soldiers or workers.
The Queen is the only female within a colony of social insects that can reproduce.
An adult eusocial insect capable of reproduction of unspecified sex (queen/gyne/drone).
Sterile members of a eusocial insect colony whose primary function is defense.
Worker insects are those within social insect colonies (bees, ants, wasps and termites) that are not capable of reproducing.

ctcrystal_habit.description: Needle-like, slender and/or tapered such as natrolite or rutile.
In mineralogy and petrology, an aggregate is a mass of mineral crystals, mineraloid particles or rock particles.
Like embedded almonds such as heulandite and subhedral zircon.
a mineral that forms long fibres that are flexible, of high tensile strength, and form in fibrous aggregates of thin crystals that readily separate.
Blade-like, slender and flattened such as actinolite and kyanite.
Globular or grape-like, hemispherical masses such as hematite, pyrite, malachite, smithsonite, or hemimorphite.
Similar to fibrous: Long, slender prisms often with parallel growth such as calcite, gypsum/selenite.
Aggregated flaky or tabular crystals closely spaced such as barite and marcasite.
Cube shape such as pyrite, galena or halite.
Also arborescent. Tree-like, branching in one or more direction from central point such as romanechite, magnesite or native copper.
Rhombic dodecahedron, 12-sided such as garnet.
Also drusy or encrustation. Aggregate of minute crystals coating a surface or cavity such as uvarovite, malachite or azurite.
Mirror-image habit (i.e. crystal twinning) and optical characteristics; right- and left-handed crystals such as quartz, plagioclase or staurolite.
Extremely slender prisms such as serpentine group, tremolite (i.e. asbestos).
Also capillary. Hair-like or thread-like, extremely fine such as many zeolites.
Also micaceous or lamellar (layered). Layered structure, parting into thin sheets such as muscovite and biotite.
Aggregates of anhedral crystals in matrix such as bornite and scheelite.
Doubly terminated crystal with two differently shaped ends such as hemimorphite and elbaite.
Hexagon shape, six-sided such as quartz and hanksite.
Like cubic, but outer portions of cubes grow faster than inner portions, creating a concavity such as halite, calcite or synthetic bismuth.
Breast-like: surface formed by intersecting partial spherical shapes, larger version of botryoidal, also concentric layered aggregates such as malachite and hematite.
Also compact massive Shapeless, no distinctive external crystal shape such as limonite, turquoise, cinnabar or realgar.
Also tuberose. Deposit of roughly spherical form with irregular protuberances such as chalcedony.
Octahedron, eight-sided (two pyramids base to base) such as diamond and magnetite.
Flat, tablet-shaped, prominent pinnacoid such as wulfenite.
Fine, feather-like scales such as aurichalcite, boulangerite or mottramite.
Elongate, prism-like: well-developed crystal faces parallel to the vertical axis such as tourmaline and beryl.
Hexagonal appearance due to cyclic twinning such as aragonite and chrysoberyl.
Also radial or divergent. Radiating outward from a central point without producing a star (crystals are generally separated and have different lengths) such as stibnite.
Also colloform. Similar to botryoidal/mamillary: intersecting kidney-shaped masses such as hematite, pyrolusite or greenockite.
Crystals forming net-like intergrowths such as cerussite.
Also lenticular (lens shaped crystals). Platy, radiating rose-like aggregate such as gypsum and, barite (i.e. desert rose).
Wedge-shaped such as sphene.
Forming as stalactites or stalagmites; cylindrical or cone-shaped such as calcite, goethite or malachite.

Star-like, radial aggregates radiating from a "star"-like point to produce gross spheres (crystals are not or weakly separated and have similar lengths) such as pyrophyllite, aragonite, wavellite and pyrite suns.
Not a habit per se, but a condition of lines that can grow on certain crystal faces on certain minerals such as tourmaline, pyrite, quartz, feldspar and sphalerite.

Bacteria refers to the mostly free-living, mostly single cell organisms that are ubiquitous occurring in every possible habitat. Bacteria that are tested in biological records are usually the pathogenic species (e.g. any of the 66 species of bacterial spirochaete that cause Leptospirosis). Specify testing methods, species and disease in Methods and Remarks.

Deoxyribonucleic acid or DNA is the double-helix polynucleotide chain carrying genetic information. Records examined for DNA may or may not have a specific target organism. Specify testing methods, any species, and results or references in Methods and Remarks.

Fungi comprise a Kingdom of eukaryotic, heterotrophic organisms including yeast, mold, and mushrooms. Records examined for fungi may not have a specific target organism. Use a more specific term if known. Specify testing methods, any species and references in Methods and Remarks.

An isotopic signature (also isotopic fingerprint) is a ratio of non-radiogenic 'stable isotopes', stable radiogenic isotopes, or unstable radioactive isotopes of particular elements in an investigated material. The ratios of isotopes in a sample material are measured by isotope-ratio mass spectrometry against an isotopic reference material. This process is called isotope analysis.

The microbiome is a community of microorganisms (microbiota) that can usually be found living together in any given habitat, such as in the digestive tract, on the skin, or in a cave deposit; includes bacteria, archaea, fungi, algae, small protists and potentially viruses and other genetic elements. For specific communities, such as fungal mycobiomes, include detail in Methods.

A parasite is an organism that benefits at the expense of another organism of a different species (the host). Use this term only when more specific information on the type of parasite is not available.

Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Fungi: Chytridiomycota: Rhizophydiales), often denoted as “Bd”, is a zoosporic fungus that causes the disease chytridiomycosis, or chytrid, (World Organisation for Animal Health Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals, 2021). The epiderma of the amphibian is the major targeted organ, with clinical signs of chytridiomycosis being skin redness and thickening, and excess sloughing of skin from the epidermal surface, especially from ventral surfaces of the abdomen, limbs and feet (Berger et al., 2005a; 2005b; Pessier et al., 1999). In extreme cases, chytridiomycosis can impact key regulatory biophysical systems, leading to weight loss, lethargy, limb locking, and eventual heart failure. Distribution of Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis and pathology in the skin of green tree frogs (Litoria caerulea) with severe chytridiomycosis. Dis. Aquat. Vet. Diagn. Invest., 11, 194–199.

Coccidioides is a genus of dimorphic ascomycete fungi in the family Onygenaceae. Member species are the cause of coccidioidomycosis, also known as San Joaquin Valley fever, an infectious fungal disease largely confined to the Western Hemisphere and endemic in the Southwestern United States.

Snake Fungal Disease (SFD) is caused by the fungus _Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola_ in the Nannizziopsiaceae within the Ascomycota. Clinical signs of SFD include: accelerated ecdysis cycles, epidermal flaking and crusting, displaced and/or discolored scales, granulomas, nodules, and swelling or disfiguration of infected tissues. ctluster.description: Adamantine minerals possess a superlative lustre, which is most notably seen in diamond. Such minerals are transparent or translucent, and have a high refractive index (of 1.9 or more).
Dull minerals exhibit little to no lustre, due to coarse granulations which scatter light in all directions, approximating a Lambertian reflector. An example is kaolinite.
Coarser, and having even less lustre than dull minerals.
A fibrous lustre is similar, but has a coarser texture.

Greasy minerals resemble fat or grease. A greasy lustre often occurs in minerals containing a great abundance of microscopic inclusions, with examples including opal and cordierite, jadeite. Many minerals with a greasy lustre also feel greasy to the touch.
Metallic (or splendent) minerals have the lustre of polished metal, and with ideal surfaces that will work as a reflective surface.  Examples include galena, pyrite and magnetite.

Pearly minerals consist of thin transparent co-planar sheets. Light reflecting from these layers give them a lustre reminiscent of pearls.[9] Such minerals possess perfect cleavage, with examples including muscovite and stilbite.
Resinous minerals have the appearance of resin, chewing gum or (smooth-surfaced) plastic. A principal example is amber, which is a form of fossilized resin.
Silky minerals have a parallel arrangement of extremely fine fibres, giving them a lustre reminiscent of silk. Examples include asbestos, ulexite and the satin spar variety of gypsum.
Minerals with a lesser (but still relatively high) degree of lustre than adamantine, some examples being garnet and corundum.

Submetallic minerals have similar lustre to metal, but are duller and less reflective. A submetallic lustre often occurs in near-opaque minerals with very high refractive indices, such as sphalerite, cinnabar, anthracite, and cuprite.

Vitreous minerals have the lustre of glass. (The term is derived from the Latin for glass, vitrum.) This type of lustre is one of the most commonly seen, and occurs in transparent or translucent minerals with relatively low refractive indices. Common examples include calcite, quartz, topaz, beryl, tourmaline and fluorite, among others.
Waxy minerals have a lustre resembling wax. Examples include jade and chalcedony.

Of or pertaining to a metacarpal bone. A bone of the hand or forefoot between the wrist and fingers; when all the digits are present ,there are five more or less elongated metacarpal bones, one at the base of each digit.

The bones of the hand or foot which connect the wrist or ankle bones to the digits. Metapodials are referred to as metacarpals in forelimbs and metatarsals in hindlimbs. The metapodials form the third segment of the leg in digitigrade and unguligrade tetrapods.

The triangular arch of bone which protrudes from the top of a vertebra. It is fused to the centrum in most mammals. The spinal cord runs between the centrum and the neural arch through a cylindrical cavity called the neural canal. The neural arch is the dorsal counterpart of the haemal arch or chevron.

When the spinous process of the neural arch exceeds the length of the transverse process, it is called a neural spine. Neural spines form the sails of animals such as Dimetrodon and Spinosaurus, as well as the humps of animals such as bison or muskoxen.

A small diploid cell which, upon maturation, forms a primordial follicle in a female fetus or the female (haploid or diploid) gametangium of certain thallophytes.

A corneous or calcareous anatomical structure like a trapdoor which exists in many (but not all) groups of sea snails and freshwater snails, and also in a few groups of land snails and some marine and freshwater gastropods. A series of bones found in bony fish and chimaeras that serves as a facial support structure and a protective covering for the gills of fish. A bone inside the clitoris of many mammalian taxa. It is homologous to the baculum in male mammals.

Bone deposits found in the skin, including bone scales, scutes, ridges, and plates. If the horn or keratinous layer is also present, the appropriate part name is scute. If both the keratinous and bony parts of the scute are present, it will be advantageous to record two parts, scute and osteoderm.
A calcium carbonate structure in the saccule or utricle of the inner ear, specifically in the vestibular system of vertebrates. Also called statoconium or otoconium or statolith.
a female reproductive organ in which ova or eggs are produced
The roof of the mouth, consisting of the structures that separate the mouth from the nasal cavity. The bony palate is composed of the following bones: premaxillae, maxillae, and palatines.

The bone which forms the posterior portion of the palate (the roof of the mouth) in advanced synapsids. The same bone has convergently evolved in archosaurs to extend the palate in a similar way. In more basal gnathostomes, the palatine bones are separate within the maxilla.
A calcified structure located at the base of the siphons in bivalve mollusks of the family Teredinidae used to seal the burrow entrance.
An organ of the digestive system and endocrine system of vertebrates.
bone which can be found in the cranium of many vertebrates. It is an unpaired dermal bone which lies at the midline of the roof of the mouth.
The two bones in the skull which, when joined together at a fibrous joint, form the sides and roof of the cranium.
The kneecap. It is found in mammals, birds, and frogs.
A hard, glistening object produced within the soft tissue (specifically the mantle) of a living shelled mollusk or another animal, such as fossil conulariids.
A mass of undigested parts of a bird's food that some bird species occasionally regurgitate.

The pelvis consists of paired hipbones, connected in front at the pubic symphysis and behind by the sacrum; each is made up of three bones—the blade-shaped ilium, above and to either side, which accounts for the width of the hips; the ischium, behind and below, on which the weight falls in sitting; and the pubis, in front.
The primary sexual organ that male animals use to inseminate females (or hermaphrodites) during copulation.
Pereiopods are primarily walking legs and are also used for gathering food. They are also the ten legs from which decapods take their name.
A membrane that covers the outer surface of all bones,[1] except at the articular surfaces (i.e. the parts within a joint space) of long bones.
The bone that surrounds the inner ear of birds and mammals, formed from the fusion of the prootic, epiotic, and opisthotic.
The foot, the terminal element of the hindlimb in tetrapods. [ Consider using foot ]

The basal element of the temporal. Part of the inner ear canal. The petrous part of the temporal bone is pyramid-shaped and is wedged in at the base of the skull between the sphenoid and occipital bones.

A bone in a finger distal to the metacarpus or in a toe distal to the metatarsus. Digital bones in the hands and feet of most vertebrates.

Gill arches found in all chordates. In advanced chordates such as gnathostomes, pharyngeal arches migrate during embryonic development to form the maxilla and mandible. In fish, the arches are known as the branchial arches, or gill arches. Highly modified elements of the pharyngeal arches also form the ear bones of mammals.
The chambered portion of the shell of a cephalopod. It is divided by septa into camerae.

Microscopic amorphous bio-silica structures that are produced within and between plant cells by precipitation and polymerization of silica. Often preserved in plant tissue or preserved in sedimentary rocks as part of the fossil record.
The distal wrist bone which articulates with the ulna.
A temporary fetal organ that begins developing from the blastocyst shortly after implantation.
The nearly flat part of the shell structure of a turtle, what one would call the belly or ventral surface of the shell.
Unspecified bones of the wrist and ankle. In digitigrade and unguligrade animals the podials form the second joint in the limb after the elbow or knee.
A fine to coarse powdery substance comprising pollen grains which are male microgametophytes of seed plants, which produce male gametes (sperm cells).
Paired cranial bone found in many tetrapods that is part of the skull roof, between and behind the eye orbits, lateral to the frontal and parietal bones, and anterior to the postorbital bone.
The cranial bone which forms the posterior rim of the orbital and connects to the frontal and squamosal bone in some archosaurs.
Fusion of the postorbital with the postfrontal.
Paired (or fused) cranial bone in many tetrapods found behind the parietal, forming the back of the skull.
A bone of the lower jaw in some tetrapods, anterior to the articular and above the angular bones.
A bone peculiar to the ornithischian dinosaurs, an unpaired beak-like bone which protrudes from the anterior tip of the dentary.

The cranial bone joined to the lacrimal and frontal bone within the skulls of sarcopterygian fishes, including tetrapods. It is absent in advanced therapsids and theropod dinosaurs, though it is prominent in both primitive dinosaurs and synapsids.
One of a pair of small cranial bones at the very tip of the upper jaw of many animals, usually, but not always, bearing teeth.
The bone between the cheek and the gill cover.
One of three cranial bones which enclose the inner ear in primitive tetrapods. It is fused with the epiotic and opisthotic bones in mammals to form the periotic bone.

In fishes, one of the cartilaginous or bony elements (as basalia and radialia) by which rays of the fin of a fish are supported. There may be three cartilages that ossify into proximal, median and distal pterygiophores (or axonost, mesonost and baseost or epibaseost).
The bone which forms the back of the palate in many vertebrates.

The pubis is the anterior element of the hip bone. In dinosaurs, the orientation of the pubis determines the classification of so-called 'bird-hipped' and 'lizard-hipped' or ornithischian and saurischian dinosaurs. In ornithischian dinosaurs the pubis runs backward along the ischium while in saurischian dinosaurs the pubis juts forward. Birds, which are saurischian dinosaurs, have secondarily evolved the ornithischian hip condition.
The posterior body part or shield of crustaceans and some other arthropods, such as insects and the extinct trilobites.
The fused caudal vertebrae of advanced birds. It is analogous to both the fused caudal vertebrae of apes, the coccyx, and the fused caudal vertebrae of frogs, the urostyle.
The fingerlike projections located near the junction of the stomach and the intestine. Also as pyloric ceca.
A square posterior element of the cranium. In advanced therapsids, including mammals, the incus is a modified quadrate.

A cranial bone found in some sarcopterygians, including some tetrapods, which connects the maxilla, squamosal, and jugal and which contacts the quadrate. The quadratojugal is reduced in primitive synapsids and entirely absent in advanced cynodonts, including mammals.

The larger counterpart of the ulna located in the lower forelimb. It is fused to the ulna in some ungulates and amphibians.

An anatomical structure used by mollusks for feeding, sometimes compared to a tongue.[2] It is a minutely toothed, chitinous ribbon, which is typically used for scraping or cutting food before the food enters the oesophagus.

Root systems that have been encased in mineral matter.Rhizoliths are created through processes of chemical weathering, decomposition, reprecipitation and cementation.
A modified subterranean plant stem that sends out roots and shoots from its nodes.
A curved element of the axial skeleton which extends down from the vertebra or up from the sternum, enclosing the body cavity, found in almost all vertebrates.
Ribonucleic acid is a polymeric molecule essential in various biological roles in coding, decoding, regulation and expression of genes.
Any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter.
The organs of a plant that are modified to provide anchorage for the plant and take in water and nutrients into the plant body.
A term for any beak-like structure, analogous of which may be found throughout the animal kingdom.

The rump. The sacrum is a number of fused sacral vertebrae associated with the hip. The number of vertebrae which comprise the sacrum varies from species to species. In theropod dinosaurs, including birds, the sacral vertebrae are further fused into adjoining caudal and lumbar vertebrae, as well as the hip bones, to form the synsacrum.
A small rigid plate that grows out of an animal's skin.
The most proximal wrist bone which connects to the radius.
The shoulder blade, the bone which connects the humerus to the clavicle.
The combination of the coracoid and scapula found in many vertebrates. Therian mammals, which lack the coracoid, do not possess a scapulocoracoid.

This term is used to describe a hard chitinous or calcareous plate, piece, scale, spine, or spicule, most typically associated corals, echinoderms, mollusks, and regions of the arthropod integument. It may be: a) Hard chitinous structure, typically associated with regions of the arthropod integument. In arthropods, these hardened plates are formed through a process known as sclerotization, which strengthens and rigidifies the chitin-protein matrix, contributing to the exoskeleton's durability and protection; b) a calcareous structure of several forms present in most octocorals species. In octocorals, the sclerites are produced by specialized cells and consist of polycrystalline aggregates of calcite deposited over a fibrous matrix. Their shape, size, and coloration can vary widely among species, playing a role in their structural support and protection. Taxonomy of octocorals relies on sclerites as diagnostic morphological characters; c) a calcareous scale or spine present on the bodies of aculiferan molluscs (aplacophorans and chitons). Their shape, size, and whether or not they are hollow vary among species and is taxonomically informative.

A component of a ring of bone which encircles the pupil. Sclerotic rings are present in many groups of vertebrates, though they are not ubiquitous in any class. Modern mammals and crocodilians entirely lack sclerotic rings.

A bony external plate or scale overlaid with horn, as on the shell of a turtle, the skin of crocodilians, and the feet of birds. If the horn or keratinous layer is not present, the appropriate part name is osteoderm along with the part modifier scute, bony. If both the keratinous and bony parts of the scute are present, it will be advantageous to record two parts, scute and osteoderm. The term is also used to describe the anterior portion of the mesonotum in insects as well as some arachnids (e.g., the family Ixodidae, the scale ticks).

A substance which accumulates through the laying down of material over time. Clastic sediments are formed when chunks entrained in a fluid, usually air or water, loose energy and settle out of the flow. Chemical sediments are formed when changes in solubility cause dissolved chemicals to precipitate out of a liquid, usually water.
An embryonic plant enclosed in a protective outer covering.

Any bone which is suspended in tendons or muscles.

For invertebrates, typically a calcareous exoskeleton which encloses, supports and protects the soft parts of an animal in the phylum Mollusca, which includes snails, clams, cephalopods, tusk shells, and several other classes. Any of various tubular organs in animals and especially mollusks or arthropods that are used for drawing in or ejecting fluids or air to be used for the purposes of locomotion, respiration, feeding, or reproduction.

An internal support structure of an animal, composed of mineralized tissue.

or small bowel is an organ in the gastrointestinal tract where most of the absorption of nutrients and minerals from food takes place. It lies between the stomach and large intestine.

The fusion of the sphenoid and ethmoid bones found in some amphibians.

A compound bone that forms the base of the cranium, behind the eye and below the front part of the brain. It has two pairs of broad lateral “wings” and a number of other projections, and contains two air-filled sinuses.

In a zoological context, spines are hard, needle-like anatomical structures found in both vertebrate and invertebrate species. The spines of most spiny mammals are modified hairs, with a spongy center covered in a thick, hard layer of keratin and a sharp, sometimes barbed tip.
An organ found in all vertebrates. Similar in structure to a large lymph node, it acts primarily as a blood filter.

The element of a crinoid that extends from the base of the calyx and anchors the crinoid to the sea floor. The individual skeletal elements of the stalk are called columnals.
Also called the stirrup, a middle ear bone present in all tetrapods. It is homologous to the hyomandibula found in teleostomi.

One of two main structural axes of a vascular plant, the other being the root. It supports leaves, flowers and fruits, transports water and dissolved substances between the roots and the shoots in the xylem and phloem, stores nutrients, and produces new living tissue.
The breastplate, a bone which is connected to and suspended by the false (ventral) ribs. In advanced birds, the sternum is keeled to allow for the attachment of large flight muscles.

A muscular, hollow organ in the gastrointestinal tract of humans and many other animals, including several invertebrates. The stomach has a dilated structure and functions as a vital digestive organ. It performs a chemical breakdown by means of enzymes and hydrochloric acid.

The bone below the operculum in the opercular series in fish.
A bone on the dorsal side of the great foramen of the skull, usually forming a part of the occipital in the adult, but distinct in the young.
A cranial element which connects the parietal and squamosal together.

The suprangular or surangular is a jaw bone found in most land vertebrates, except mammals. Usually in the back of the jaw, on the upper edge, it is connected to all other jaw bones: dentary, angular, splenial and articular.
An absorbent pad or piece of material. Should be accompanied by part attribute(s) specifying where and how the swab was used.
The fusion of the sacral vertebrae, hip bones, as well as nearby caudal and lumbar vertebrae. A bone found in theropod dinosaurs, including birds.
A complex vocal organ found in some birds, analogous to mammalian vocal folds in function but not in form. Some elements of the syrinx are mineralized.
One of a pair of triangular flat bones along the rear edge of the skull which form pointed structures known as tabular horns in primitive Teleostomi.

The tail is the section at the rear end of certain kinds of animals’ bodies; in general, the term refers to a distinct, flexible appendage to the torso. It is the part of the body that corresponds roughly to the sacrum and coccyx in mammals, reptiles, and birds; for fish, the area between the anterior end of the anal fin to the anterior end of the caudal fin . While tails are primarily a feature of vertebrates, some invertebrates including scorpions and springtails, as well as snails and slugs, have tail-like appendages that are sometimes referred to as tails.

Bones of the ankle located between the metatarsals (foot bones) and the fibula and tibia (lower hindlimb bones). Tarsals form the second 'knee' joint in digitigrade and unguligrade tetrapods. Present in all sarcopterygian fishes, including tetrapods. These bones are also known as the tarsus collectively.

Testicle or testis (plural testes) is the male reproductive gland or gonad in all animals.
The middle section of the body of an insect, between the head and the abdomen, bearing the legs and wings.
Also known as the shinbone or shankbone, is the larger, stronger, and anterior (frontal) of the two bones in the leg below the knee in vertebrates that connects the knee with the ankle bones.
The fusion of the tibia and fibula. Found in some amphibians.
The fusion of proximal elements of the tarsus and the tibia. Found only in theropod dinosaurs.
An ensemble of similar cells and their extracellular matrix from the same origin that together carry out a specific function.
Any of the digits of the foot of a tetrapod.

Sediment preserving impressions left by organisms. Often a type of ichnofossil or a trace fossil. (See Donovan, S.K. (2025), The significance of traces and trace fossils: trails, burrows and borings. Geology Today, 41: 56-60. )

The tympanic part of the temporal bone is a curved plate of bone lying below the squamous part of the temporal bone, in front of the mastoid process, and surrounding the external part of the ear canal.
The smaller counterpart of the radius located in the lower forelimb. It is fused to the radius in some ungulates and amphibians.
In placental mammals, a conduit between the developing embryo or fetus and the placenta.
Also known as the hamate. A hook shaped wrist bone.
A distal phalanx (a fingertip or toetip) which has been modified to support a nail, claw, or hoof.

A long unsegmented bone that represents a number of fused vertebrae and forms the posterior part of the vertebral column of frogs and toads.
Also womb, a major female hormone-responsive secondary sex organ of the reproductive system in humans and most other mammals.

Also mating plug, copulation plug, sperm plug, sement or sphragis. A gelatinous secretion used in the mating of some species. It is deposited by a male into a female genital tract, such as the vagina, and later hardens into a plug or glues the tract together.
A type of poison, especially one secreted by an animal.
The gizzard, gigerium, or gastric mill, is an organ found in the digestive tract of some animals including birds, reptiles, and some invertebrates.
Contents of the ventriculus (gizzard, gigerium, or gastric mill), an organ found in the digestive tract of some animals including birds, reptiles, and some invertebrates.

An irregular bone in the vertebrate spinal column with a complex structure composed of bone and some hyaline cartilage, the proportions of which vary according to the segment of the backbone and the species of vertebrate.
An intervertebral disc (or intervertebral fibrocartilage) lies between adjacent vertebrae in the vertebral column.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, consider part=hair and appropriate modifiers. ] Also whiskers. A type of stiff, functional hair used by animals to sense their environment.
[ BEST PRACTICE: Do not use, consider part=unknown and appropriate modifiers. ] An unspecified internal organ of the body.

one of the unpaired facial bones of the skull. It is located in the midsagittal line, and articulates with the sphenoid, the ethmoid, the left and right palatine bones, and the left and right maxillary bones.
an anatomical structure that connects the swim bladder to the auditory system in fishes belonging to the superorder Ostariophysi
A contiguous alive or once living physical entity; entity or being that is or was living; an individual living or once living thing, such as one animal, plant, fungus, or bacterium.
A type of appendage that produces lift while moving through air or some other fluid.
A porous and fibrous structural tissue found in the stems and roots of trees and other woody plants.
Also articular processes. Projections of the vertebra that serve the purpose of fitting with an adjacent vertebra. The actual region of contact is called the articular facet.
A bone which forms the distal ridge of the eye socket.

ctsubject_term.description: Designates buildings or groups of buildings that are abandoned by their owners, often constituting potential public hazards. In a legal connotations, the term does not include buildings that are temporarily vacant or unoccupied.

Genre of visual arts in which figurative subjects or other forms are simplified or changed in their representation so that they do not portray a recognizable person, object, thing, etc.; may reference an idea, quality, or state rather than a concrete object. For the process of formulating general concepts by abstracting common properties of instances, prefer "abstraction." For 20th-century art styles that were a reaction against the traditional European conception of art as the imitation of nature, use "Abstract (fine arts style)."

The state of being physically or psychologically habituated to a substance or practice to such an extent that its cessation causes severe trauma. For the long term or excessive use or misuse of narcotics, alcohol, or other substances, use "substance abuse."

Nontechnical term for heavier than air fixed-wing aircraft designed to utilize the pressures created by their motion through the air to lift and transport people and cargo; if possible use a more precise term.

Typically refers to large tracts of open, level land upon which runways, hangars, terminals, and other buildings have been constructed to allow for the takeoffs, landings, loading and unloading, and maintenance of aircraft. For smaller areas that have a runway but no or few additional facilities, see "airfields."
Artists who identify as Athabascan, Inupiaq, Northwest Coast (Haida, Tlingit, Tshimshian,), St. Lawrence Island Yupik, Sugpiaq (Alutiiq), Yup’ik and/or Unangan (Aleut).
Projectiles and propellants used to operate firearms.
Discipline concerned with the structure, function, and development of the cells, tissues, and organs constituting the animal body.

Kingdom containing multicellular organisms having cells bound by a plasma membrane and organized into tissue and specialized tissue systems that permit them to either move about in search of food or to draw food toward themselves. Unable to make their own food within themselves, as photosynthetic plants do, they rely on consuming preformed food. They possess a nervous system with sensory and motor nerves, enabling them to receive environmental stimuli and to respond with specialized movements.

Scientific study of the material remains of past human life and activities, including human artifacts from the very earliest stone tools to the man-made objects that are buried or thrown away in the present day. Archaeological investigations are a principal source of knowledge of prehistoric, ancient, and extinct cultures.

The Arctic is a polar region located at the northernmost part of Earth. The Arctic consists of the Arctic Ocean, adjacent seas, and parts of Alaska (United States), Finland, Greenland (Denmark), Iceland, Northern Canada, Norway, Russia and Sweden. Land within the Arctic region has seasonally varying snow and ice cover, with predominantly treeless permafrost (permanently frozen underground ice) containing tundra. Arctic seas contain seasonal sea ice in many places.
Common term for several poplar trees that are typically native to cold regions with cool summers, in the north of the Northern Hemisphere but extending south at high altitudes in the mountains.
Natural light display in the Earth's sky, predominantly seen in the high-latitude regions around the Arctic.
Self-propelled vehicles designed primarily to transport passengers over ordinary roads.
The season of the year which is the transition period from summer to winter, occurring as the sun approaches the winter solstice, its beginning marked by the autumnal equinox.

Agricultural buildings with large, usually sliding doors, prominent roofs, and predominantly open spaces on the interior, primarily used as storage buildings for hay, grains, and farm equipment and shelters for livestock; does not include those structures, often termed barns, used for the processing of food and other agricultural produce, such as hop barns and tobacco barns.
Establishments with counters where beverages, usually liquors, and light meals are served to customers.
Process of creating containers made of twigs, rushes, thin strips of wood, or other flexible material woven together.
Containers made of twigs, rushes, thin strips of wood, or other flexible material woven together.
The washing of humans or animals; for recreational immersion in water, use "swimming."
Shores comprised of an accumulation of sediment, such as sand or pebbles, along the edge of a sea or lake, and formed by coastal processes such as waves and tides.

Ursidae (family) - Family containing nine species in six genera, characterized as being large, short-tailed, having stocky legs, a long snout, shaggy hair, and plantigrade paws with five non-retractile claws. Bears are generally omnivorous, but some bears are entirely carnivorous (like the polar bear ) or vegetarian (like the panda).

Castor - Members of a genus containing two living species of amphibious rodents native to North America, Europe, and Asia. Beavers have short legs, a stout body, a small, broad, blunt head, large chisel-shaped incisor teeth, a broad, oval, horizontally-flattened, scaly tail, palmated hind feet, and a coat of soft fur. They are distinguished by their ability to chew through trunks and cut down trees, constructing huts of mud and wood for habitation, and dams for preserving a supply of water.

Bell-shaped jars, placed open-end down on a base and usually sealed, for display or storage of artifacts, natural specimens, dried flower arrangements, figurines, objets d'art, or other decorative items. For bell-shaped glass covers used to protect living plants, use "bell glasses (horticultural containers)."

The beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas) is an Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean. It is one of two members of the family Monodontidae, along with the narwhal, and the only member of the genus Delphinapterus. It is also known as the white whale, as it is the only cetacean to regularly occur with this colour; the sea canary, due to its high-pitched calls; and the melonhead, though that more commonly refers to the melon-headed whale, which is an oceanic dolphin.

A berry is a small, pulpy, and often edible fruit. Typically, berries are juicy, rounded, brightly colored, sweet or sour, and do not have a stone or pit, although many pips or seeds may be present. Common examples are strawberries, raspberries, blueberries, blackberries, red currants, white currants and blackcurrants. In Britain, soft fruit is a horticultural term for such fruits.
Two hundredth anniversaries or their observances.

Betula (genus) - Genus of hardy, deciduous trees of the family Betulaceae, common to North America, Europe and Asia. Birch tress are readily distinguished by their white bark and diamond-shaped leaves. The lightweight bark contains natural waxes, oils, and tannins that make it tough, durable, and waterproof. Thin sheets of bark were commonly used for paper in Central Asia and the Far East. The water-impervious bark was used for wigwams, canoes, and shoes for Native Americans. Birch produces a strong, pale yellow-brown wood with a close, straight grain and uniform texture that finishes to a smooth surface. Dyes can also be obtained from various parts of birch trees. The leaves, usually gathered before they develop a mature green color, produce a yellow dye. The bark produces a pale brown color. The female catkins (a long shoot bearing flowers with no leaves) are boiled to produce a dull yellow color. Birch bark oil and birch beer are made from sap obtained from the trees. The sap allows birch bark to burn even when it is wet.

Aves - The class of vertebrate animals that are typically bipedal and warm-blooded, lay large-yolked hard-shelled eggs, often arboreal, and possessing feathers, hollow bones, forelimbs adapted for flight (although some have lost the ability to fly) and hindlimbs for perching and locomotion, a four-chambered heart, keen vision, a horny beak without teeth, and a large muscular stomach. Birds arose from theropod dinosaurs, which were an order of carnivorous dinosaurs.

Ursus americanus - Medium-sized bear native to North America. It is the continent's smallest and most widely distributed bear species. American black bears are omnivores, with their diets varying greatly depending on season and location. They typically live in largely forested areas, but do leave forests in search of food.

Nalukataq is the spring whaling festival of the Iñupiat of Northern Alaska, especially the North Slope Borough. It is characterized by its namesake, the dramatic Eskimo blanket toss. "Marking the end of the spring whaling season," Nalukataq creates, "a sense of being for the entire community and for all who want a little muktuk or to take part in the blanket toss....At no time, however, does Nalukataq relinquish its original purpose, which is to recognize the annual success and prowess of each umialik, or whaling crew captain....Nalukataq [traditions] have always reflected the process of survival inherent in sharing...crucial to...the Arctic."

Blood quantum laws or Indian blood laws are laws in the United States and the former Thirteen colonies that define Native American identity by percentages of ancestry. These laws were enacted by the American government, by contrast many tribes and nations do not include Blood Quantum (BQ) as part of their own enrollment criteria. A person's blood quantum is defined as the fraction of their ancestors, out of their total ancestors, who are documented as full-blood Native Americans.

Hue name for one of the three primary additive colors; that portion of the spectrum lying between green and violet, with a wavelength of about 420 to 490 nanometers, which is the shortest wavelength range of the three primary colors. The term may refer to any of this group of colors that vary in lightness and saturation. An example of blue color in nature is that of a clear sky during the day.
Watercraft generally smaller and less seaworthy than ships and generally not designed to cross large open waters.

Designates waterlogged spongy ground with a characteristic plantlife, such as sphagnum mosses, and in which vegetation is decaying, ultimately producing highly acidic peat. Distinct from "fens," in which the water remains alkaline.

The rigid, calcareous material that is white in color and forms the skeleton of vertebrates; primarily composed of calcium hydroxyapatite with smaller amounts of calcium carbonate, calcium fluoride, magnesium phosphate, and ossein, a high molecular weight protein. Bones have a concentric structure with central lymphatic canals surrounded by a spongy lamellar region protected by a dense outer cortex. Bone has been carved and used since ancient times for many purposes, including fish-hooks, spear heads, needles, handles, and art objects. Bones were also burnt to produce bone black and boiled to produce bone glue. Bone can be distinguished from ivory by being generally whiter, more porous, and less dense.
Drawings created specifically to be included in a published book.

Items comprising a collection of leaves of paper, parchment, wood, stiffened textile, ivory, metal tablets, or other flat material, that are blank, written on, or printed, and are strung or bound together in a volume.
Drawings, prints, or other pictures that illustrate plants and their parts, often accurately rendered from life.

The bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus) is a species of baleen whale belonging to the family Balaenidae and the only living representative of the genus Balaena. It is the only baleen whale endemic to the Arctic and subarctic waters, and is named after its characteristic massive triangular skull, which it uses to break through Arctic ice. Other common names of the species are the Greenland right whale or Arctic whale. American whalemen called them the steeple-top, polar whale, or Russia or Russian whale.

Stringed projectile weapons designed to propel arrows, generally consisting of a long stave of wood, metal, fiberglass, or other flexible material, with a length of strong string fastened to the tips of the stave which is bent in a curve, either permanently or from the tension of the string. The string is drawn back, holding the arrow by means of a notch in its rear tip, and propels the arrow upon release.
Structures spanning and providing passage over waterways, topographic depressions, transportation routes, or similar circulation barriers.
Ursus arctos - Members of a species containing over 20 subspecies and up to 80 varieties of shaggy-haired bear native to Europe, Asia, and northwestern North America.
Structures, generally enclosed, that are used or intended to be used for sheltering an activity or occupancy.
Rough buildings often with bunk beds, used for sleeping quarters, as for ranch hands, migratory workers, and campers.
The buntings are a group of Old World passerine birds forming the genus Emberiza, the only genus in the family Emberizidae. They are seed-eating birds with stubby, conical bills.
Following slaughter, the extraction of meat from animals for consumption; the trade of a butcher.
Small dwellings characteristic of the frontier or other rustic area, especially when built by non-professionals from available logs or stones.
A small shed elevated on poles above the reach of animals and used for storing food, equipment, etc.

Plant family including more than 2,000 species, grouped into around 175 genera, although classification is much debated. Most species are native to the New World, found the length of North and South America. It is debated whether or not they are true cacti, but some species may possibly be found in East Africa, Madagascar, and Sri Lanka.

A campfire is a fire at a campsite that provides light and warmth, and heat for cooking. It can also serve as a beacon, and an insect and predator deterrent. Established campgrounds often provide a stone or steel fire ring for safety. Campfires are a popular feature of camping. At summer camps, the word campfire often refers to an event (ceremony, get together, etc.) at which there is a fire. Some camps refer to the fire itself as a campfire.
Lightly built, slender, open craft of shallow draft that are paddled and not rowed and normally double-ended; may have sails.

Rangifer tarandus - Species of deer with large branching or palmated antlers, formerly common in Central Europe, but now confined to sub-arctic regions of Europe and North America; commonly domesticated and used for hauling, meat, milk, and skins.

The act of shaping, marking, or decorating wood, stone, or another material by cutting or incising, typically using tools such as chisels and other blades. It refers to this process as it is applied to small-scale objects or to objects that are not considered art. "Carving" may also be considered a sculpture technique that is employed in the creation of art.

Felis domesticus - Domesticated member of the genus Felis, rising from a line that developed 70,000/100,000 years ago. Domesticated in Egypt ca. 2,000 BCE, in Cyprus by 9,500 years ago, earlier elsewhere in the Middle East. In some taxonomies, Felis domesticus and Felis sylvestris are the same species. Genetic evidence suggests that the domestic cat developed from an ancestor who also produced the subspecies of wild cat, Felis sylvestris lybica. The house cat appears to have been domesticated in the Middle East at a time when humans recognized its value in protecting fields and granaries from rodents. Egyptian affection and respect for the cat as predator led to the development of religious cat cults and temple worship of cats. Since tabby-like markings appear in the drawings and mummies of ancient Egyptian cats, present-day tabbies probably look much like the sacred cats of Egypt. The first known domestic variation on the wild tabby coloring was the black cat (which also occurs naturally in the wild, but not in great numbers). The darker tabby coat with thicker stripes and swirls probably first appeared in the Middle Ages, the coat pattern being an adaptation that helped the animal to hide better in the shadows of dark medieval streets. The tortoise shell coat probably developed in the 19th century, when the Victorians made cats beloved pets and bred them for color varieties and other characteristics. Until the recent genetic studies, some experts believed the domestic cat was a hybrid of Felis Sylvestris and an Egyptian forest cat that was more docile and also kept in some Egyptian temples.
A collective term referring to live animals, particularly bovine animals, held as property or reared to serve as meat, or sources of milk, skin, wool, etc.
Large, subterranean, naturally formed chambers, with entrances from the surface.

Events demonstrating grateful or happy satisfaction or honor, marked by festivities, refraining from ordinary business, or other deviations from accustomed routine. For events serving specifically to call someone or something to remembrance, use "commemorations."

In general, areas used for burial or entombment. Specifically, typically refers to relatively large public parks or grounds laid out expressly for the interment of the dead, and not being the yard of any church. Originally the term was derived from the Latin "cœmeterium," referring to Roman underground cemeteries or catacombs.

The chickadees are a group of North American birds in the tit family included in the genus Poecile. Species found in North America are referred to as chickadees, while other species in the genus are called tits. They are small-sized birds overall, usually having the crown of the head and throat patch distinctly darker than the body. They are at least 6 to 14 centimeters (2.4 to 5.5 inches) in size.
The earliest developmental stage of a living being.
People in the earliest developmental stage of life.
Art produced by children.

Refers to the world religion and culture that developed in the first century CE, driven by the teachings of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. Its roots are in the Judaic tradition and the Old Testament. The tenets include a belief in the death and redemptive resurrection of Jesus. The religion incorporates a tradition of faith, ritual, and a form of church authority or leadership.
Institutions that maintain places for public Christian worship.

Performances that include trained animal acts or exhibitions of human skill and daring, or both. Circuses usually include a trained, traveling company or troupe of performers, various animals, and their equipage. The term "circus" refers to the circular arena surrounded by tiers of seats below which the performance occurs in a circular area called the "ring."

Distinctions among villages, towns, and cities are relative and vary according to their individual regional contexts. Towns generally are units of compact settlement larger than villages and less important and internally complex than cities in the region.
Removing dirt, surface coatings, accretions, discolorations, or other undesired matter from a substrate.

Any alteration in regional or global climate as during the five glacial periods of the past 450,000 years. The term is often applied to the recent changes in global climatic patterns, attributed to emission of greenhouse gases, also known as global warming.
Visible masses of condensed water vapor floating in the air at some considerable height above the general surface of the ground.
The practice or policy of control by one people or power over other people or areas, often by establishing colonies and generally with the aim of economic dominance.

An extraterrestrial body consisting of a frozen mass and rock debris that travels around the Sun in a highly elliptical orbit; it generally developes a diffuse gaseous envelope and a long luminous tail when near the Sun.

Places where construction is occurring, particularly construction of a building. For the more general meaning of a site where a building is or was located, whether or not the building is under construction, use "building sites."
The process of preparing food, a dish, or a meal, typically by combining and heating ingredients.

General term referring to any of over 1,300 species of invertebrate marine organisms of several genuses of the class Anthozoa (phylum Cnidaria) that are characterized by internal or external skeletons that have a stonelike, horny, or leathery consistency. In most species, the skeletons are joined together in massive colonies; they feed on small fish and invertebrate plankton using stinging cells on outstretched tentacles, and reproduce both sexually or by budding. For the calcium carbonate skeletal material produced by some species, use "coral (material)."

Populus trichocarpa, the black cottonwood, western balsam-poplar or California poplar, is a deciduous broadleaf tree species native to western North America. It is used for timber, and is notable as a model organism in plant biology. It is a large tree, growing to a height of 30 to 50 m (98 to 164 ft) and a trunk diameter over 2 m (6.6 ft), which makes it the largest poplar species in the Americas. It is normally fairly short-lived, but some trees may live up to 400 years.

Gruidae (family) - Members of a family containing 15 living species of tall wading birds with very long legs, neck, and bill. Cranes resemble herons but are usually larger and have a partly naked head, a heavier bill, more compact plumage, and an elevated hind toe. Cranes are ancient in origin, found in Eocene deposits in North America.
Living or animate beings, including animals or people that are fantastic or of anomalous or uncertain aspect or nature.
Bodies of water, smaller than a stream.
General term applied to many of the 40 species of glossy black birds in the genus Covus, although some birds in this genus are called "ravens" rather than crows.
Crustacea (subphylum) - Members of a subphylum containing crabs, lobsters, shrimps, barnacles, and many other forms.
